headline: 60% of Google app installs were robots for developer's $220 ad spend
summary: A puzzle app developer discovered that over half of the installs generated by their Google Ads campaign were bots, despite Google Play being reported as the installer source.
details: A puzzle app developer spent CA$220 on Google Ads for his app, Dayzle, aiming for installs. He discovered that 60% of the billed installs were actually bots, not real users.

Initially, Google Ads struggled to find installs at the target cost per install. After removing the target, it spent double the daily budget, reporting 21 installs, but the developer's own analytics showed only one.

Upon deeper investigation, 20 new Android devices were found running old app versions, which the Play Store had stopped serving days prior. Despite this, all reported Google Play as the installer. These "users" opened the app once, spent zero seconds on any screen, and never returned.

Over two weeks, 56 installs were billed. Of these, 33 followed the suspicious bot pattern, 7 came from countries not targeted by the campaign, and only 13 were real people who genuinely played the game.

The developer suspects a bot farm, which would watch the shortest ad video without clicking, then install the app from a saved copy. This method is faster and less likely to be detected by the Play Store.

Ironically, Google's algorithm counted a view followed by an install as a conversion, leading it to send more ads to the bot farm. This created a loop that guaranteed the ad spend was wasted on fake installs.

The developer has since changed the campaign goal to "won a puzzle" to make bot farming more costly. He is currently awaiting Google's response to an invalid-traffic form and plans to report on any refund.
This serves as a public service announcement: developers relying on Google's install counts should investigate thoroughly, as bot farms can target even small ad budgets.

headline_marked: [[EPA plans to scrap public review rules]] for data center pollution permits
headline: EPA plans to scrap public review rules for data center pollution permits
summary: The EPA is proposing to remove public review for air pollution permits for industrial facilities, including data centers, and allow construction before permits are approved. This could worsen health risks and increase utility bills in affected communities.
details: The federal Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) plans to eliminate a requirement that states inform the public and allow comments before approving air-pollution permits for industrial facilities. This includes the numerous data centers and their power plants being built across the country.

Additionally, the EPA proposed another change last month that would permit developers to begin constructing data centers even before their necessary permits are officially approved. This accelerates development without prior regulatory clearance.

These changes disproportionately affect the rural South, home to many Black communities, which has seen the largest growth of large data centers. Residents fear increased health risks, higher utility bills, and potential community displacement.

The federal changes mean that in some areas, residents could lose their only formal opportunity to raise concerns or even learn about a new data center before permits are finalized and construction commences. This reduces transparency significantly.

The proposals face strong opposition, with nearly 200 advocacy groups and over a dozen states, including both Democrats and Republicans, voicing their disapproval. Environmental activists describe these moves as a "betrayal of everything this country should stand for."

A growing pattern of secrecy surrounds these projects, with local governments often signing non-disclosure agreements with tech companies. They have also reportedly overruled legal orders to conceal information about data center developments.

Data centers contribute to environmental burden by driving demand for gas-fired power plants and turbines. These facilities emit smog-forming nitrogen oxides, fine particulate matter, and hazardous air pollutants like formaldehyde, linked to various cancers.
